item.content:encoded:
UK government says it is minded to intervene in Sky-ITV deal Reuters | Updated: 15-10-2026 18:08 IST | Created: 15-10-2026 18:08 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

British culture minister Lisa Nandy said on Thursday she was minded to intervene in Comcast's Sky deal to buy the broadcast channels and streaming service of Britain's ITV for £1.6 billion ($2.1 billion). Nandy said she had potential concerns about the deal's impact on the breadth of news providers in Britain, as well as the extent of Sky's control over the media. She told the two companies she would also examine whether the deal could reduce the availability of high-quality programmes appealing to a wide variety of tastes and interests. That concern would extend to on-demand as well as broadcast content, and would require an amendment to the existing grounds for intervention to reflect new viewing habits, she said. Sky agreed in July to buy ITV's broadcast business, home to programmes such as "Coronation Street", national news provided by ITN and popular regional news shows. Sky already owns rival news provider Sky News, as well as sports and entertainment channels. ITV Chief Executive Carolyn McCall said at the time she expected the deal to be subject to a lengthy review. The two companies have until October 20 to respond to Nandy's concerns. ($1 = 0.7550 pounds)

item.title: Tibetan leader raises concerns over China’s religious interference, Dam projects at Prague Democracy Forum
item.description: Sikyong Penpa Tsering, head of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), raised concerns over China’s alleged suppression of Tibetan identity, interference in Buddhist religious traditions and ...
item.content:encoded:
Tibetan leader raises concerns over China’s religious interference, Dam projects at Prague Democracy Forum Sikyong Penpa Tsering, head of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), raised concerns over China’s alleged suppression of Tibetan identity, interference in Buddhist religious traditions and environmental policies during the 30th Forum 2000 Conference in Prague, according to a report by the CTA. ANI | Updated: 15-10-2026 17:32 IST | Created: 15-10-2026 17:32 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Sikyong Penpa Tsering, head of the Central Tibetan Administration (CTA), raised concerns over China’s alleged suppression of Tibetan identity, interference in Buddhist religious traditions and environmental policies during the 30th Forum 2000 Conference in Prague, according to a report by the CTA. On the second day of the conference, held at the Prague Congress Centre, Tsering attended the opening plenary session and participated in a panel titled “Václav Havel’s Courage of the Powerless.” He also held bilateral meetings with German Bundestag member Roderich Kiesewetter and Japanese House of Representatives member Yuya Mineshima. During an interview with Milan Kajínek of The Epoch Times, as cited by CTA, Tsering criticised Beijing’s “Ethnic Unity Law” and the use of boarding schools, alleging that these measures were designed to assimilate younger generations of Tibetans. He also rejected the Chinese Communist Party’s claims to authority over the Dalai Lama’s reincarnation, questioning how an atheist regime could determine Buddhist succession. Tsering warned that China’s dam construction and environmental policies on the Tibetan Plateau could threaten regional food and water security. Describing Tibet as the “Water Tower of Asia,” he highlighted concerns over Beijing’s refusal to share hydrological data and the potential consequences for downstream communities. He also cautioned Western democracies against excessive economic dependence on China, warning that Beijing could seek to expand its model of authoritarian surveillance internationally. According to the CTA, Tsering subsequently met Ana Helena Chacón, former Vice President of Costa Rica, and held discussions with international figures, including Freedom House President and CEO Jamie Fly, European Parliament member Alexandr Vondra, and Robert Řehák, chair of the International Religious Freedom or Belief Alliance. In the afternoon, Tsering participated as a keynote panelist in “When Faith Becomes Political: Defending Freedom in an Age of Authoritarianism,” organised in cooperation with the Community of Democracies. The discussion was moderated by its Secretary General, Mantas Adomėnas, and also featured academic Grace Davie and His Beatitude Epiphanius I of Ukraine. During the session, Tsering outlined the CTA’s diplomatic outreach to democratic governments, Buddhist communities and the Tibetan diaspora. He cited the 1995 disappearance of the 11th Panchen Lama, Gedhun Choekyi Nyima, as an example of what he described as China's interference in Tibetan religious affairs. He maintained that recognition of the next Dalai Lama rests exclusively with the India-registered Gaden Phodrang Trust. He also criticised China's Order No. 5 and the use of the Golden Urn in reincarnation procedures, while reiterating the CTA’s commitment to the Middle Way Approach, which seeks genuine autonomy for Tibet. Tsering called on the international community to adopt stronger resolutions protecting the Dalai Lama’s reincarnation process and supporting Tibetans’ rights, the CTA report stated. He later spoke with Czech Radio’s Noemi Fingerlandová, discussing the relationship between Václav Havel and the Dalai Lama, environmental concerns and international support for Tibet. He also met an Iranian delegation comprising civil society representatives, human rights advocates and academics. Tsering concluded the day by attending the Global Democracy Networking Dinner at the Grand Hotel Prague Towers. He was accompanied throughout the engagements by Representative Thinlay Chukki and Phuntsok Topgyal, UN Advocacy Officer at the Tibet Bureau in Geneva, according to the CTA. (ANI)

item.title: Pakistan ranks worst in South Asia on 2026 Global Hunger Index as food insecurity deepens
item.description: Pakistan has recorded the worst performance in South Asia in the 2026 Global Hunger Index, highlighting the country’s deepening food insecurity amid economic instability, soaring food prices, ...
item.content:encoded:
Pakistan ranks worst in South Asia on 2026 Global Hunger Index as food insecurity deepens Pakistan has recorded the worst performance in South Asia in the 2026 Global Hunger Index, highlighting the country’s deepening food insecurity amid economic instability, soaring food prices, climate-related disasters and international conflicts, as reported by Dawn. ANI | Updated: 15-10-2026 17:01 IST | Created: 15-10-2026 17:01 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Pakistan has recorded the worst performance in South Asia in the 2026 Global Hunger Index, highlighting the country’s deepening food insecurity amid economic instability, soaring food prices, climate-related disasters and international conflicts, as reported by Dawn. According to Dawn, the report, under the theme “No Security Without Food Security”, was jointly prepared by Welthungerhilfe, the Institute for International Law of Peace and Armed Conflict at Ruhr University Bochum, and Swiss organisation Helvetas. The findings indicate that hunger reduction across South Asia has largely stalled, with Pakistan and Afghanistan experiencing worsening conditions since 2018. Pakistan’s economic difficulties and rising food inflation have weakened household purchasing power, leaving many families struggling to afford adequate nutrition. The country’s undernourishment indicator has worsened from a low level in 2018 to a medium level, while child wasting has approached the threshold for the high category. South Asia’s overall Global Hunger Index score stands at 23.5, placing the region in the serious category. Although the score has improved from 37.5 in 2000, much of the progress occurred before 2018. Pakistan and Afghanistan have moved out of the alarming category over the past two decades, but persistent child malnutrition remains a major concern. Child stunting continues to decline in Pakistan, whereas Afghanistan has witnessed a slight increase since 2018. Child mortality has improved in both countries, falling from very high levels in 2000 to medium levels currently. The report also highlighted the impact of extreme weather on regional food production. Heavy rainfall and flooding damaged crops in parts of Pakistan and Bangladesh, while insufficient rainfall and unusually high temperatures affected Afghanistan’s cereal-growing season in 2026. These climate pressures could prolong acute food insecurity, as highlighted by Dawn. Estimates from the Food and Agriculture Organisation suggest that 218 million people across South Asia, including Iran, suffered from undernourishment between 2023 and 2025, accounting for approximately one-third of the global total, as reported by Dawn. (ANI)

item.title: India's exports to US rise 11%, imports jump 26% amid ongoing trade talks
item.description: India's merchandise exports to the United States rose 11.1 per cent to USD 50.81 billion during April–September 2026, despite tariff-related disruptions, while imports from the US increased by 26 per ...
item.content:encoded:
India's exports to US rise 11%, imports jump 26% amid ongoing trade talks India's merchandise exports to the United States rose 11.1 per cent to USD 50.81 billion during April–September 2026, despite tariff-related disruptions, while imports from the US increased by 26 per cent, according to data presented by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Thursday. ANI | Updated: 15-10-2026 15:41 IST | Created: 15-10-2026 15:41 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

India's merchandise exports to the United States rose 11.1 per cent to USD 50.81 billion during April–September 2026, despite tariff-related disruptions, while imports from the US increased by 26 per cent, according to data presented by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry on Thursday. Exports to the US increased from USD 45.73 billion in the corresponding period last year, while imports rose to USD 32.33 billion from USD 25.66 billion. The figures show that bilateral trade continued to expand despite tariff uncertainties, although India's merchandise trade surplus with the US narrowed to USD 18.48 billion from USD 20.07 billion a year earlier. The US remained India's largest merchandise export destination during the first half of the current financial year. Meanwhile, Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said negotiations for the proposed India-US trade agreement were progressing in the right direction, with both countries working towards concluding the deal at the earliest. "The negotiations are in the right direction. Probably, we are in a very good zone. We anticipate closing the deal and signing it at the earliest possible time," Agrawal said during a press briefing. He explained that the agreement would depend on the finalisation of the broader tariff framework in the United States, where a parallel process is underway under Section 301. "The deal has to be signed when the overall tariff structure is getting formalised. There is parallel work being done in the US also to get back the tariff structure based on some of the outcomes of the 301," he said. Agrawal further emphasised that India was seeking preferential access to the American market to ensure its exporters could compete effectively with other countries. "When you do a trade deal, it gives you not only market access in each other's markets; it gives you preferential market access in a particular market," he said. He added that India's preferential market access relative to its competitors would form part of the new tariff framework. The ongoing negotiations are significant as both countries seek to strengthen bilateral trade ties while addressing tariff-related challenges affecting market access. (ANI)
